_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications.
rashi:a1.1: That one does not administer punishment on the basis of an a fortiori inference: for we do not say: Just as [the Torah] punished for his sister from the father alone, or from the mother alone, [for his sister] from the father and from the mother, all the more so.
rashi:a2.1: And if you wish, say: [even if,] according to Rabbi Yitzḥak, one does not administer punishment on the basis of an inference, Rabbi Yitzḥak derives the punishment for his sister from his father and from his mother in that he learns punishment from the warning: just as [the Torah] warned about her as about the other forbidden relatives, so it punished for her. Her warning is explained in tractate Makkot (14a): the verse states, “The nakedness of your father’s daughter or your mother’s daughter”; I have only your father’s daughter who is not your mother’s daughter, and your mother’s daughter who is not your father’s daughter. From where [do I know] your father’s daughter who is also your mother’s daughter? The verse states: “She is your sister; you shall not uncover her nakedness.” And just as it warned about her, so it punished for her.
rashi:a3.1: Rabbi Elazar said: divide the sin offerings: so that if he did both of them in one lapse of awareness, he is liable to two.
rashi:a4.1: Karet with regard to his sister: which the verse spelled out for her separately; what does it come for?
rashi:a4.2: A gloss: Since the prohibitions [themselves] divide, [the verse] is not needed to divide for his sister who is his father’s sister and his mother’s sister, for she has three prohibitions.
rashi:a4.3: This is the reading: “According to Rabbi Yitzḥak, per his opinion; the Rabbis require it for his sister who is his father’s daughter and his mother’s daughter, to say that one does not administer punishment on the basis of an inference.” And the whole verse comes because of “his sister” in the latter clause; for the sake of a single new point it is the way [of the Torah] to repeat a passage that was already stated.
rashi:a4.4: “According to Rabbi Yitzḥak he requires it,” etc., up to “the latter clause”: we do not have this in our text; it is a corrupt explanation from mistaken students. End of the gloss. [The passage meant appears to be the one in our printed Gemara that runs from “According to Rabbi Yitzḥak, he derives” to “in the latter clause,” shown in the next few messages.]
rashi:a8.1: And one is liable for it by itself: for each one, when he does them in one lapse of awareness.
rashi:a10.1: The tanna, what is he counting? Now, we said above that the count comes for this: that if he did all of them [in one lapse of awareness he is liable for each one]. How can you find thirty-four sin offerings in one [person]?
rashi:a11.1: A man: it is he who copulates with an animal.
rashi:a11.2: A woman: for example, where she had intercourse with her son, and with her husband’s son, and with her father-in-law, and with her son-in-law, and with an animal; and likewise all of them.
rashi:a11.3: One who has intercourse with a male and with an animal: for there is no woman’s side to these. As for the Paschal offering and circumcision, he cannot raise an objection from them, for [the tanna] did not list them on account of sin offerings, since they are not subject to an offering at all: an offering comes only for a prohibition, as is explained below.
rashi:a12.1: And it is Rabbi Yishmael: [as stated] in the chapter Arba Mitot [of Sanhedrin].
rashi:a13.1: But from the fact that it teaches the blasphemer among those liable to karet, to teach us that he brings an offering, and we establish it below in accordance with Rabbi Akiva, who said at the end of our chapter (Keritot 7a) that a blasphemer brings an offering, the first clause too is Rabbi Akiva.
rashi:a14.1: As Rabbi Abbahu said: in the chapter Arba Mitot (Sanhedrin 54b). “There shall not be a sodomite” is the warning for the one who is lain with, and the punishment comes from a verbal analogy, as it is written: “And there were also sodomites in the land” [I Kings 14:24]. And if you ask: with the other forbidden relations, where do we find a warning for the woman as for the man, since with all of them we find the prohibition [addressed to the man]? One answers thus: there it is different, since she too derives pleasure from the lying, “the souls that do them” [Leviticus 18:29] applies to her. But in male intercourse, where [the one lain with] does not derive pleasure, a warning is needed. And [the verse] is written with regard to men, for there is no “male” with an animal, and it is not called sodomy.
rashi:a18.1: Rabbi Elazar said: he counts with regard to men. And as for your difficulty about the woman who is the object of bestiality: the tanna counted thirty-three sin offerings for one man in one lapse of awareness, and taught the woman with an animal, the Paschal offering and circumcision to complete the [list of] karet.
rashi:a20.1: And the soul that does with a high hand: the verse is speaking of idol worship.
rashi:a21.1: Just as idol worship is “sit and do not act”: and one is liable to karet for its intentional violation and a sin offering for its unwitting violation, as it is written just before: “a she-goat in its first year for a sin offering” [Numbers 15:27].
rashi:a21.2: So too every “sit and do not act”: whose intentional violation carries karet and whose unwitting violation carries a sin offering.
rashi:a23.1: They are forty less one: [so] let it teach seventy-five cases of karet.
rashi:a23.2: He taught unwitting with regard to Shabbat: that he thinks today is a weekday.
rashi:a23.3: And intentional with regard to labors: that he knows these labors are forbidden on Shabbat. Even if he did all the primary labors he is liable only one, since there is only one error. And our mishna lists the cases of karet by the liability for a sin offering.
rashi:a24.1: “Them” that is “one”: as it is written, “and performs from one of them [me’aḥat mehena]”; it could have written “one of them [aḥat mehena]”; what does “from one [me’aḥat]” mean? Sometimes from a single transgression one is liable “them,” that is, several sin offerings; and “from them [mehena]”: for many transgressions, one sin offering.
rashi:a24.2: Unwitting with regard to Shabbat and intentional with regard to labors: and he did many labors; he is liable only one.
rashi:a25.1: Intentional with regard to Shabbat: that he knows today is Shabbat.
rashi:a25.2: And unwitting with regard to labors: that he does not know these labors are forbidden, but he knows the mitzva of Shabbat in one matter, for example, he knows it is forbidden to go out beyond the Shabbat limit.
rashi:a26.1: “One” that is “them”: for one mitzva, such as Shabbat, he is liable several sin offerings.
rashi:a27.1:
Unwitting with regard to Shabbat and intentional with regard to labors is preferable to him: to teach us a new point, that even though he acted intentionally with regard to the labors, he is not exempt from one sin offering.
Another version: unwitting with regard to Shabbat and intentional with regard to labors is preferable to him because it is a categorical ruling: once he erred about Shabbat he is not exempt from at least one sin offering, for even if he also erred about the labors he is liable one. But unwitting with regard to the labors, so that he is liable for each and every one, is not categorical, for sometimes he is exempt from that liability, for example where he also erred about Shabbat, so that he was unaware of both, and we say in tractate Shabbat (70b) that he is liable only one.
And it is reasonable that [the mishna] speaks of unwitting with regard to Shabbat, since for idol worship the mishna counts one and no more. By inference it speaks of unwitting with regard to idol worship and intentional with regard to the rites; for if it were unwitting with regard to the rites, there would be four sin offerings for the four rites: slaughtering, burning incense, pouring a libation and bowing.
rashi:a29.1: His heart is toward Heaven: for even if he bowed to Heaven in a house of idol worship, he did nothing forbidden, and there is no sin offering.
rashi:a30.1: This is the reading: “If he did not accept it upon himself as a god, it is nothing”: since it was not done for the sake of idol worship, his bowing is nothing.
rashi:a31.1: Rather: he bowed to an idol out of love for a person or fear of a person, for he thought it is permitted to worship an idol out of love and fear. And it is called intentional with regard to the rites, since he means to worship.
tosafot:a1.1:
In brief: To say that one does not administer punishment on the basis of an a fortiori inference: This is puzzling, since above “his sister” was needed to divide the offerings for a sister who is also his father’s sister, so he is liable at least one; why, if one does not punish by inference? Answer: he learns it from here, since the verse revealed it here.
But below, in chapter 3 (13b), the mishna rules “There is one who eats a single eating and is liable” to several offerings; why, if perhaps the graver case is not liable? And one cannot learn it from here, for a sister is unique in that she was never permitted out of her general prohibition. Some answer: here there is only the prohibition of his sister, a sister on two sides being graver than on one, so one does not punish by inference; there, other prohibitions take effect through the rules of an inclusive prohibition, an added prohibition and prohibitions taking effect at once.
It is puzzling: why, for his daughter from the woman he raped, does the Gemara (Sanhedrin 77a) derive it a fortiori from his daughter’s daughter, treating it as merely revealing the matter and not as a warning derived by inference? Answer: a daughter’s daughter comes through the relationship of his daughter and cannot exist without her, whereas a sister can be his father’s daughter and not his mother’s, or the reverse. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:a14.1: According to Rabbi Yishmael, who derives it, etc.: This is puzzling: how is the mishna to be explained? Karet is not written with “There shall not be a sodomite”; so how can there be liability for a sin offering for it? One can say: since karet is written for male intercourse, it is two prohibitions and one karet.
tosafot:a22.1: To complete the cases of karet: This is puzzling: if so, let it also count “brought a male upon himself” and “brought an animal upon himself.”
gershom:a1.1: Divide the sin offerings between them: even though a sin offering comes only where there is karet, even so, since two prohibitions are written and one karet, it implies karet for each prohibition. And since prohibitions divide the sin offerings, the same applies to forbidden relations, which have many prohibitions and one karet. So why was karet with regard to his sister needed? And Rabbi Yitzḥak holds that “his sister” at the start of the verse is not for exposition but is the manner of the verse, needed for itself: “a man who takes his sister”; and “sister” at its end he needs to divide. And if you ask: why does Rabbi Yitzḥak say “his sister” in the first clause is the manner of the verse, when he derives from it that the sinner is judged with karet and not with lashes? He derives that only from “karet,” not from “his sister.” And our teacher told us that it is the Gemara in tractate Makkot that brings this “if you wish, say: he derives the punishment from the warning” with regard to Rabbi Yitzḥak, who says one administers punishment on the basis of an inference. It says: if you wish, say: for his sister who is his father’s daughter and his mother’s daughter, he derives the punishment from the warning and not from an inference, for a warning is written for her, as it is written: “The nakedness of your father’s wife’s daughter, born to your father” [Leviticus 18:11], and he derives the punishment from the warning. Here it cannot be explained so, because the Rabbis do not derive punishments from warnings in this way; rather, they need karet with regard to his sister to say that one does not administer punishment on the basis of an inference.
gershom:a2.1: We too learned it: in accordance with Rabbi Elazar’s statement in the name of Rabbi Oshaya that prohibitions divide [the sin offerings].
gershom:a3.1: For just as the incense is an independent prohibition, as it is written: “And the incense that you shall make, according to its composition you shall not make” [Exodus 30:37], and one is liable for it by itself, as it is written: “Whoever shall make like it, to smell it, shall be cut off” [Exodus 30:38].
gershom:a4.1: And if you say there is no proof from this, for he taught “one who blends the incense” in the middle because he wants to teach the two blendings next to each other: if so, let him teach them in the reverse order.
gershom:a5.1: If he is counting men: that if thirty-six men committed these thirty-six cases of karet, each would be liable to karet; if so, remove the woman who is the object of bestiality from among them.
gershom:a6.1: If he is counting women: that if thirty-six women committed them, each would be liable to karet.
gershom:a7.1: Remove from them one who has intercourse with a male and with an animal: for these can be explained only with men, and two are lacking from them. And if you mention circumcision too, that does not apply to women [either].
gershom:a8.1: This is not difficult, for it speaks only of prohibitions. [A note in the printed text: it appears it should read: Actually he counts men, and as for your objection “remove the woman who is the object of bestiality,” teach thus in its place, etc.] And teach thus: remove the woman who is the object of bestiality, and teach in its place: “and brought a male upon himself,” which is one who is lain with by a male.
gershom:a9.1: And it is Rabbi Yishmael, who says he is liable to two, since he derives it from two verses, as is said below. But from the fact that it teaches the blasphemer among these, and we explain it in accordance with Rabbi Akiva, who does not require an action, the first clause too is Rabbi Akiva; and Rabbi Akiva holds that one who has intercourse with a male and brought a male upon himself is liable only one. If so, one is lacking from them.
gershom:a10.1: And if you say the whole mishna is Rabbi Akiva, and in the first clause, about one who has intercourse with a male, Rabbi Akiva holds like Rabbi Yishmael that he is liable to two. And “There shall not be a sodomite” means that he should not be lain with like a prostitute.
gershom:a11.1: And according to Rabbi Akiva: who derives it from one verse, he is liable only one.
gershom:a12.1: Evidently he does not hold like Rabbi Yishmael. Rather, the first clause and the latter clause are Rabbi Yishmael, and with regard to the blasphemer he holds like Rabbi Akiva, who does not require an action, even though it is written “when [she] does” and “and does one.”
gershom:a13.1: If so: according to Rabbi Yishmael, who holds him liable to two, let it also teach “and brought an animal upon himself,” and add one.
gershom:a14.1: Didn’t Abaye say, etc.: this is the answer. And when “There shall not be a sodomite” is written, it is written with regard to men: that he should not be lain with by a person; [it does] not [speak of] an animal. And the reason why here, with a male, a warning is needed for the one lain with, which is not so with the other forbidden relations, is that with the other forbidden relations one warning suffices for both, since the one lain with derives pleasure like the one who lies; with one who has intercourse with a male, the one lain with does not derive pleasure.
gershom:a15.1: Rabbi Elazar said in the name of Rava [our Gemara reads: Rav]: Actually he counts men, and there is no need to remove the woman who is the object of bestiality, for the tanna taught thirty-three sin offerings and taught three cases of karet that carry no sin offering, to complete them, filling out the thirty-six cases of karet. And from where [do we know] he taught cases of karet without sin offerings? From the fact that the latter clause teaches the Paschal offering and circumcision, which carry no sin offering, since they are mitzvot of “arise and do.”
gershom:a16.1: The entire Torah is juxtaposed to idol worship: because “he has despised the word of the Lord” [Numbers 15:31], that is, he despised the first utterance, “You shall have no [other gods].” And the tanna also taught karet for the woman who is the object of bestiality to complete [the list]: since it does not apply to men, it carries no sin offering.
gershom:a17.1: And those others, which are prohibitions and apply to men, carry karet and a sin offering.
gershom:a18.1: One who desecrates Shabbat: he counts it as one karet. They say: but Shabbat has thirty-nine cases of karet, for its primary labors.
gershom:a19.1: Rabbi Yoḥanan said: our tanna, who counts one who desecrates Shabbat as one karet, is speaking of unwitting with regard to Shabbat and intentional with regard to labor, as it is taught: “them” that is “one”: when he did many labors and is liable only one. That is unwitting with regard to Shabbat and intentional with regard to labor: he does not know it is Shabbat but knows these labors are forbidden on Shabbat; and since he did them intentionally, knowingly, there is no offering for them except for the error about Shabbat alone. And why does he explain “one who desecrates Shabbat” as speaking of unwitting with regard to Shabbat and intentional with regard to labor, where he is liable only one? Let it teach intentional with regard to Shabbat and unwitting with regard to labor, where he would be liable thirty-nine, etc.
gershom:a20.1: The tanna of the mishna prefers to teach unwitting with regard to Shabbat and intentional with regard to labor, to teach us a greater point: that even though he acted intentionally with regard to the labors, he is not exempt from at least one sin offering. Another version: that is why he prefers it [a note in the printed text: it appears it should read: for even if he also erred about the labors, in any case he is not exempt from one, to exclude, etc.], for whether he erred about Shabbat … [the printed text is unclear here] … to exclude intentional with regard to Shabbat and unwitting with regard to labor, for if he also acted intentionally with regard to the labor he is entirely exempt from a sin offering.
gershom:a21.1: And likewise you find with regard to one who worships an idol, whom the mishna teaches is liable only one: because it speaks of unwitting with regard to idol worship and intentional with regard to the rites.
gershom:a22.1: And his heart is toward Heaven: for he thinks it is a synagogue, and he is not liable for anything.
gershom:a23.1: Rather, where he saw an andarta, a statue not made for the sake of idol worship, and bowed to it: what unwitting sin is there here, since it is not an idol? The matter depends on this: if he accepted it [as a god], he acted intentionally; and if he did not accept it, he did nothing and is not liable.
gershom:a24.1: Rather, for example, where he erred about idol worship, thinking it is permitted to worship it because he does so only out of love of a ruler or out of fear. And intentional with regard to the rites [the printed text corrects “labors” to “rites” here]: there is no intentional sin with the rites here, since he did not act intentionally; rather it is called “intentional with regard to the rites” because he means to worship out of love.
gershom:a25.1: This works out well according to Abaye, who says he is liable: one who worships out of love or fear; and the mishna is explained in this way, as unwitting with regard to idol worship.
rashi:b1.1: Rather, where he says it is permitted: to worship idols; that is, unwitting with regard to idol worship and unwitting with regard to the rites.
rashi:b1.2: For Rava raised a dilemma before Rav Naḥman only: what is [the halakha where] he was unaware of both this and that? In the chapter Arba Mitot (Sanhedrin 62a).
rashi:b2.1: Rav Pappa said: you find it in a child who was taken captive among the gentiles: unwitting with regard to idol worship and intentional with regard to the rites; for example, where he later heard that the idol that is there is forbidden with these four rites, and most people know these rites are forbidden.
rashi:b3.1: Unwitting with regard to idol worship: he thinks there is no [forbidden] idol of wood.
rashi:b4.1: Rav Aḥa son of Rav Ika said in the name of Rav Beivai: Actually, [the mishna] also counts intentional with regard to Shabbat and unwitting with regard to the labors. And as for what you said, “let it count more”: the tanna goes over only the mitzvot for which one is liable to karet.
rashi:b4.2: He teaches the category of Shabbat, he teaches the category of idol worship: and in fact each one contains many.
rashi:b4.3: But there is his daughter from the woman he raped, which is not written: rather, it is derived from “hena” “hena” and from “zimma” “zimma,” in tractate Ḥagiga at the end of the first chapter (11a).
rashi:b7.1: Rav Aḥa raised a contradiction: between Rav Beivai and Rav Beivai.
rashi:b7.2: But wasn’t it stated: in tractate Zevaḥim, in the chapter HaShoḥet (107a).
rashi:b7.3: Inner limbs: of an animal slaughtered in the Temple courtyard.
rashi:b7.4: Outer limbs: a consecrated animal slaughtered outside.
rashi:b8.1: And it was difficult for Rav Beivai: there, in Zevaḥim: if so, that there are two kinds of offering up, let it teach in Keritot: one who offers up inner limbs outside the courtyard, and also one who offers up outer limbs.
rashi:b9.1: Are Shabbat [and idol worship] comparable? The reckoning of the liabilities of Shabbat is taught in tractate Shabbat (73a), and that of idol worship in tractate Sanhedrin (60b).
rashi:b9.3: And with regard to karet, where it is needed: it is merely incidental that he counts them among the mitzvot for which one is liable to karet, so one can answer “the category of Shabbat, the category of idol worship.”
rashi:b9.4: But with regard to offering up: we do not find a place for it in which the mishna teaches the two kinds of offering up.
rashi:b10.1: Rabbi Yirmeya raised a dilemma, etc., what is [the halakha]? If he did them in one lapse of awareness, is he liable one or two? Do [separate] karet punishments divide the sin offerings as prohibitions do, or not?
rashi:b10.2: Slaughtering and offering up: there are two karet punishments in [the passage of] Aḥarei Mot, and one prohibition in Re’eh: “Take heed to yourself lest you offer up your burnt offerings in every place” [Deuteronomy 12:13], and wherever it says “take heed,” “lest” or “do not,” it is nothing but a prohibition. But for slaughtering there is no explicit prohibition, for the verse written in that passage (Leviticus 17:7), “And they shall no more sacrifice their sacrifices,” etc., is explained in Zevaḥim, in the chapter HaShoḥet VeHaMa’aleh (Zevaḥim 106a), as referring to one who sacrifices an animal to Markulis.
rashi:b11.1: A verbal analogy: there, in Zevaḥim: with slaughtering, “bringing” is stated: “and to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting he did not bring it”; and with offering up it is stated (Leviticus 17:9): “and to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting he does not bring it.” Just as there, with offering up, [the Torah] both punished and warned [so too with slaughtering].
rashi:b13.1: And there you shall do: [this] too [refers to] slaughtering.
rashi:b14.1: A necromancer and a sorcerer: there are two death penalties, as it is written (Leviticus 20:27): “a necromancer or a sorcerer shall be put to death”; “or” divides: whichever one he does, he shall die. And there is one prohibition, as it is written: “There shall not be found among you,” etc., “or one who consults a necromancer or a sorcerer” [Deuteronomy 18:10–11]. And they are subject to an offering, since karet is written for them (ibid. [Leviticus 20:6]): “And the soul that turns to the necromancers.” And you are asking whether death penalties divide the sin offerings, so that one who did both in one lapse of awareness is liable to two, or not.
rashi:b15.1: This is the dispute of Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish: in [the chapter] Elu Hen HaNiskalin, in Arba Mitot (Sanhedrin 65a), where we learn that for the two of them one is liable only one [sin offering], since they were stated in one prohibition; therefore there is no division of sin offerings between them. That is why [the mishna] counts only one of them, for all the cases of karet in our mishna were taught for the count of sin offerings, as we said at the beginning of our chapter: if he did all of them in one lapse of awareness he is liable for each one.
rashi:b17.1: Since it does not involve an action: therefore it is not subject to an offering. But the necromancer’s sin involves an action, for he knocks with his arms and speaks from his armpits.
rashi:b17.2: A sorcerer [yidde’oni] puts the bone of an animal called yadua into his mouth, and it speaks.
rashi:b18.1: For they are divided with regard to death penalties: and were it not for the reason that it involves no action, the death penalties would divide the sin offerings, since they are divided in the death penalties; and [the tanna] would have taught them [both] had it been subject to an offering.
rashi:b19.1: It is Rabbi Akiva, who said: below (Keritot 4a) that the blasphemer brings an offering, for we do not require an action.
rashi:b20.1: Granted, he does not require a significant action: as is clear from the fact that it teaches the blasphemer.
rashi:b22.1: It entered our mind: since Reish Lakish said that knocking his arms is an action, and we see in the mishna that the Rabbis dispute about the blasphemer but do not dispute about the necromancer, conclude from it that even according to the Rabbis it counts as an action.
rashi:b26.1: Its karet: the karet of the blasphemer. The verse speaks of the offering for idol worship in the portion Shelaḥ Lekha, “And if a soul sins unwittingly, he shall offer a she-goat in its first year,” etc. [Numbers 15:27], and in that same passage it is written, “But the soul that does with a high hand,” etc., “shall be cut off” [Numbers 15:30], which speaks of the blasphemer. It might enter your mind that, since it is written in the place of the offering, he should be liable to an offering even though it involves no action; [the mishna] teaches us: “excluding the blasphemer.”
rashi:b27.1: Ulla said: this is the reason the Rabbis do not dispute about the necromancer: [the mishna] is not speaking of the knocking of his arms but of one who burns incense to the prince of the demons.
rashi:b27.2: In order to join him: so that he will join him and help him in his sorcery; he did not burn incense to him as a god.
rashi:b28.1: That is a ḥover ḥever: and that carries neither karet nor death, only a prohibition.
rashi:b28.2: A ḥover ḥever such as this: one who burns incense to the prince of the demons.
rashi:b29.1: Both one who joins large ones: who joins large beasts and binds them together.
rashi:b29.2: And small ones: over small beasts he whispers and joins them together by sorcery.
rashi:b29.3: Even a hornet and a scorpion: though they are insignificant, it is forbidden to whisper [charms] over them.
tosafot:b14.1: Perhaps two death penalties, etc.: “they shall be put to death … their blood shall be upon them” [Leviticus 20:27]. The fact that “they shall be put to death” is written in the plural does not imply a division, for with forbidden relations too “they shall be cut off” is written in the plural, and even so a verse was needed to divide.
tosafot:b17.1: Since it does not involve an action: This is puzzling: above it said the tanna taught three cases of karet to complete the list of karet, so evidently [he taught them] even though they carry no liability for a sin offering. So too, let him teach the sorcerer, which at least carries karet.
tosafot:b29.1: And if they are pursuing him, it is permitted: This is puzzling: what are the circumstances? If there is danger, it is obvious, for nothing stands in the way of saving a life; and if there is no danger, why is it permitted?
gershom:b1.1: Rather, unwitting with regard to idol worship, what are the circumstances? Where he says it is permitted, not knowing that it is forbidden to worship idols. And intentional with regard to the rite, what are the circumstances, if he does not know it is forbidden? Since he intended to worship, they call it intentional. This is like [the case where] he was unaware of both this and that: of [idol worship] itself and of its rites.
gershom:b2.1: And why is he liable to a sin offering? [A note in the printed text: up to here belongs to 3a.] For Rava raised a dilemma before Rav Naḥman, in the chapter Kelal Gadol, only where he was unaware of both this and that, not knowing that it was Shabbat and not knowing that the labors are forbidden, whether he is liable two: if you say we follow the error about Shabbat, he is liable only one; and if you say we follow the error about the labor and not about Shabbat, he is liable for each and every primary labor.
gershom:b3.1: But to exempt him completely, he did not ask him. Here too, with regard to idol worship, he is not completely exempt, and he is liable one.
gershom:b4.1: Rav Pappa said: how do you find “where he says it is permitted”? For example, a child who was taken captive as a minor among the gentiles, who knows that idol worship is forbidden but does not know which rites are forbidden.
gershom:b5.1: And if you wish, say: you can find “where he says it is permitted” even with an adult who was [not] taken captive, for example, where he erred about this verse, etc.
gershom:b6.1: Rav Aḥa son of Rav Ika said: the tanna of the mishna teaches the category of Shabbat and the category of idol worship without specifying; that is to say, if he acted intentionally with regard to Shabbat and unwittingly with regard to labor he is liable for each and every one, and if unwittingly with regard to Shabbat and intentionally with regard to labor he is liable only one.
gershom:b7.1: From where [do we know] that the tanna taught the category of a prohibition and left cases out? From the fact that it teaches one who has intercourse with a woman and her daughter, and left out his daughter from the woman he raped, which he does not teach with them.
gershom:b8.1: They say: there is no proof from this. He teaches those written in the verse, and he did not leave out his daughter from the woman he raped; since it is not written explicitly but is derived from a verbal analogy, he does not teach it.
gershom:b9.1: [The comment opens with the abbreviation ל״א, usually “another version.”] But there are his wife’s daughter, her son’s daughter and her daughter’s daughter, which are written in the Torah and are liable to karet, and he left them out and does not teach them; rather, he teaches the category of “a woman [and her daughter],” and these too are included in it. Here too, etc.
gershom:b10.1: But wasn’t it stated: in tractate Zevaḥim: one who offers up inner limbs, which are fit to be burned in the courtyard, and burned them outside; and outer limbs: limbs of consecrated animals that he slaughtered outside and offers up outside; or he offers up non-sacred meat outside for the sake of consecrated offerings; [there are] two [liabilities]. And it was difficult for Rav Beivai:
gershom:b11.1: There: if so, that he is liable to two, there would be thirty-seven cases of karet; let it teach “one who offers up” and “one who offers up” twice, that is, once for inner limbs outside and once for outer limbs outside. And why was it difficult for him? Since he holds that [the tanna] teaches the category of Shabbat, let him answer for himself: here too he teaches the category of offering up, and the same applies to outer limbs outside.
gershom:b12.1: Rav Beivai would say to you: are they comparable? Shabbat and idol worship, he taught them bekhonkheihon, in their places; that is, each one he taught in its own tractate, all its labors and all its laws. Therefore with regard to karet here [the printed text reads de’oraita], that is, he mentioned them incidentally because he needed them, so he answers “he teaches the category of Shabbat,” and did not want to take the trouble to spell them out, since they are already spelled out in their places. But here, with offering up, did he teach them in their places? That is, is there a tractate called “tractate of offerings up” where they are spelled out, so that he could answer “he teaches the category of offering up”? Rather, since they have no tractate, he would have needed to spell out here “one who offers up” and “one who offers up”; that is what was difficult for Rav Beivai.
gershom:b13.1: Two karet punishments and one prohibition, what is [the halakha]? Do two karet punishments divide the sin offerings as prohibitions do, or not?
gershom:b14.1: He said to him: What are you asking? Are you perhaps speaking of one who slaughters and offers up outside, which carry two karet punishments? With slaughtering karet is written: “and to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting he did not bring it” [Leviticus 17:4]; and with offering up karet is written: “who offers up a burnt offering or a sacrifice, and does not bring it to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting,” etc. [Leviticus 17:8–9]. These are two prohibitions. [Either] according to the one in tractate Zevaḥim who says [it is derived from] “bringing,” “bringing”: “he did not bring it,” “he does not bring it”: just as there, with offering up, [the Torah] did not punish unless it warned (and where did it warn? As it is written: “Take heed to yourself lest you offer up your burnt offerings” [Deuteronomy 12:13], and wherever it says “take heed,” “lest” or “do not,” that is a prohibition), so too with slaughtering it did not punish unless it warned; so they are two prohibitions, and therefore they divide. Or according to the one who derives it by juxtaposition to a prohibition, as the verse states: “There you shall offer up your burnt offerings, and there you shall do” [Deuteronomy 12:14], which is slaughtering, since they are written together; conclude from it a juxtaposition that juxtaposes slaughtering to offering up: just as with offering up it did not punish unless it warned, etc., as we said, so these too are two prohibitions, and obviously they divide. And if you say a prohibition is written for slaughtering, “And they shall no more sacrifice their sacrifices” [Leviticus 17:7], we explain that as referring to one who sacrifices an animal to Markulis.
gershom:b15.1: Rather, perhaps you are asking about two death penalties and one prohibition: whether death penalties divide the sin offerings. And what is that? A necromancer and a sorcerer, for whom two death penalties are written, “shall surely be put to death; they shall stone them with stones” [Leviticus 20:27], and one prohibition, as it is written: “There shall not be found among you,” etc., “or one who consults a necromancer or a sorcerer” [Deuteronomy 18:10–11]. He said to him: Yes. Rabbi Zeira said to him: This is the dispute of Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish whether they divide or not, for we learned in Sanhedrin, with regard to stoning, “a necromancer and a sorcerer,” but with regard to karet he does not teach the sorcerer, only the necromancer. What is different that he does not teach the sorcerer? Rabbi Yoḥanan said: since both were stated in one prohibition, “There shall not be found”; since they have only one prohibition they do not divide, and that is why he teaches one.
gershom:b16.1: And let him teach the sorcerer in the mishna and not teach the necromancer; what is different that he teaches the necromancer?
gershom:b17.1: He holds: since the verse opened with it, for throughout the Torah [the verse] puts the necromancer before the sorcerer.
gershom:b18.1: And Reish Lakish said: since it does not involve an action: the sorcerer, for he only puts the yadua bone in his mouth and the bone speaks by itself, without the twisting of his lips; therefore there is no division for it. But if there were an action in it, they would divide, even though [there is] one prohibition.
gershom:b19.1: Reish Lakish, what is the reason he does not say like Rabbi Yoḥanan, as he says, that both were stated in one prohibition, are equal to each other and have no division?
gershom:b20.1: Rav Pappa said: Reish Lakish holds that since they are divided in [their] death penalties, “shall surely be put to death,” they would be divided for sin offerings if the sorcerer’s sin involved an action.
gershom:b21.1: And Rabbi Yoḥanan would say to you: a division of death is not a division for an offering, for what does a sin offering come for? For a prohibition. A division of prohibition, if they had two prohibitions, would be a division for an offering; now, since they have only one prohibition and two death penalties, a division of death is not a division.
gershom:b22.1: A division of death is not a division: for once he has died he does not die again. And this is why [the verse] states it for both of them: it might enter your mind that he is not put to death until he does both of them; it teaches us that whichever one he does, he is liable to stoning.
gershom:b23.1: And Rabbi Yoḥanan, what is the reason he does not say like Reish Lakish, that they are not divided for that reason, because they involve no action?
gershom:b24.1: He holds: Rabbi Yoḥanan [says]: who taught the mishna of Keritot? It is Rabbi Akiva, who says we do not require an action, for even when there is no action in it [a note in the printed text: it appears it should read: and even when there is no action in it, in any case there is liability for a sin offering, as he holds, etc.] (there is no division of sin offerings), as he holds with regard to the blasphemer, that he is liable to a sin offering even though there is no action in it, as we explained the mishna in the discussion above. Therefore my reason that they have no division is that both were stated in one prohibition.
gershom:b25.1: And Reish Lakish would say to you: I certainly hold like the Rabbis, who require an action. But even if the mishna is Rabbi Akiva, as you say, it is still not difficult for me: granted that Rabbi Akiva does not require a significant action as the Rabbis do, he requires at least a minor action, which excludes the sorcerer, whose sin involves no action at all, not even a minor one; and therefore there is no division. And the necromancer, according to Rabbi Akiva, what minor action does his sin involve? The knocking of his arms: he knocks his arms against each other and speaks from between his armpits and from the joints of his arms, by sorcery.
gershom:b26.1: And the blasphemer’s sin involves a minor action: the twisting of his lips.
gershom:b27.1: It entered our mind: that the knocking of his arms is, according to Reish Lakish, a minor action even according to the Rabbis, since the Rabbis do not dispute about the necromancer as they dispute about the blasphemer.
gershom:b28.1: They raise an objection, etc.: let it teach, for the Rabbis, “excluding the blasphemer and the necromancer,” whose sins involve no action. Yes, that is so; [he could have taught both] had he wished, but he teaches only one of the two, “excluding the blasphemer,” and the same applies to the necromancer.
gershom:b29.1: And let it teach “excluding the necromancer,” and not teach “excluding the blasphemer.”
gershom:b30.1: It was necessary [to teach] the blasphemer: it might enter your mind that since its karet is written in the place of an offering, as it is written above, “And it shall be, if it was done unwittingly, hidden from the eyes of the congregation” [Numbers 15:24], I would say the Rabbis concede to Rabbi Akiva that a minor action counts as an action and he is liable to an offering; it teaches us that this is not so, and that is why it teaches “excluding the blasphemer.”
gershom:b31.1: Ulla said: the necromancer that the mishna teaches is liable to a sin offering according to all is one who burns incense to a demon so that it will cause him to speak from between his armpits; and burning incense is a significant action.
gershom:b32.1: If so: one who burns incense to a demon, that is idol worship.
gershom:b33.1: Rather: where he burns incense to a demon not as worship but in order to join it, so that it will come to him and gather for him many demons who will do his will.
gershom:b34.1: If so, that is a ḥover ḥever: one who gathers groups of beasts and of snakes by sorcery, which carries only a prohibition.
gershom:b35.1: He said to him: even though one who burns incense to a demon in order to join it, for the purpose of necromancy, is a ḥover, and a ḥover ḥever carries a mere prohibition, the Torah said: a ḥover ḥever such as this [is a necromancer], for the necromancer is [punished] with stoning, and if unwitting, [brings] a sin offering.
gershom:b36.1: Both one who joins large ones: who gathers groups of large beasts.
gershom:b37.1: And one who joins small ones: who gathers small beasts.
gershom:b38.1: And even snakes and scorpions: for he is liable for the prohibition “There shall not be found [among you].”
gershom:b39.1: Abaye said: even one who joins them in order to bind a hornet and a scorpion together, so that they press against each other and kill each other, is forbidden.
gershom:b40.1: And if they are coming after him: that is, they want to harm him, and for that reason he joins them so that they will not harm him, it is permitted.
gershom:b41.1: The twisting of the blasphemer’s lips should, according to the Rabbis, be an action; so why do they say “excluding the blasphemer”?
